## Definition
Let $G$ be a graph, and let $D$ and $A$ be the degree matrix and adjacency matrix of $G$ respectively. Then the ***graph Laplacian*** of $G$ is the $n \times n$ matrix $L$ given by

$$L = D - A.$$

Specifically, the $ij$ entry of $L$ is given by

$$L_{ij} = \begin{cases} d_i & \text{if } i = j \\ -1 & \text{if } i \neq j \text{ and } v_i \sim v_j \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

or 

$$L_{ij} = \delta_{ij} d_i - A_{ij}$$

where $\delta_{ij}$ is the Kronecker-delta.

## Diffusion
본래 확산이란 기체와 같은 유체, 혹은 열에너지가 밀도와 압력 차이에 의해 높은 곳에서 낮은 곳으로 이동하며 퍼져나가는 물리적 현상을 일컫는다. 한편 이러한 현상의 메커니즘을 그대로 유지하되 그래프 이론에 적용하는 방식으로 재해석해보려 한다. 

그래프 $G$가 주어졌을 때 각 정점 $v_i$에 어떤 물질이 $\psi_i$ 만큼 존재한다고 하자. 이때 $v_j$에서 $v_i$로 물질이 흘러들어올 때 확산하는 비율은 $C(\psi_j - \psi_i)$와 같이 쓸 수 있다. $v_j$에서 $v_i$로 흘러들어오는 상황이라면 $v_j$에서 더 밀도가 높다는 뜻이고, 자연스럽게 양의 비율로 측정되는 효과를 준다. 반대로 $v_j$로 물질이 빠져나가는 상황이라면 $v_i$에서 더 밀도가 높다는 뜻이고, 역시나 자연스럽게 음의 비율로 측정되는 효과를 준다. $C$는 ***diffusion constant***로 주어지는 상수이다.

이제 $dt$라는 작은 시간이 흘렀을 때 $v_i$에서 물질의 변화율, 다시 말해 $\frac{d \psi_i}{dt}$를 알고 싶다면 모든 $j$에 대해서 위 비율을 더해주면 되고, 따라서 다음의 식이 성립한다.

$$\frac{d \psi_i}{dt} = C \sum_{j} A_{ij} (\psi_j - \psi_i)$$

$A$는 그래프 $G$의 인접 행렬이다. 한편 위 식은 다음과 같이 조작되고, 이러한 과정에서 그래프 라플라시안 $L$이 정의된다.

$$\begin{align*}
\frac{d \psi_i}{dt} &= C \sum_{j} A_{ij} (\psi_j - \psi_i) \\
&= C \sum_j A_{ij} \psi_j - C \psi_i \sum_j A_{ij} \\
&= C \sum_j A_{ij} \psi_j - C \psi_i d_i \\
&= \sum_j (A_{ij} - \delta_{ij} d_i) \psi_j \\
&= - C \sum_j L_{ij} \psi_j \\
&= - C [L \psi]_i
\end{align*}$$

여기서 $\psi = [\psi_1 \,\, \cdots \,\, \psi_n]^T$로 정의하면 마지막 식은 다음과 같은 1계 연립 상미분방정식이 된다.

$$\frac{d \psi}{dt} + C L \psi = 0$$

이때 그래프 라플라시안 $L$은 실대칭행렬이므로 에르미트 행렬이고, 따라서 대각화가능하다. $L$의 고유값과 고유벡터들을 각각 $\lambda_i, \mathbf{v}_i$라고 하면 위 미분방정식의 해는 상수 $c_i$들에 대하여 다음과 같이 주어지고, 적절히 초기조건이 주어진다면 완벽하게 해를 결정할 수 있다. 

$$\psi(t) = e^{-CtL} \psi(0) = \sum_{i} c_i e^{-C\lambda_i t} \mathbf{v}_i$$

## Edge Incident Matrix
Let $G$ be a graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges. let us arbitrarily designate one end of each edge to be end $1$ and the other to be end $2$. (It doesn’t matter which end is which, only that they have different labels.) The ***edge-incidence matrix*** $B$ of $G$ is the $m \times n$ matrix whose $ij$ entry is given by 

$$B_{ij} = \begin{cases} +1 & \text{if end 1 of } e_i \text{ is attached to } v_j \\ -1 & \text{if end 2 of } e_i \text{ is attached to } v_j \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

각 에지의 양 끝에 $1$번, $2$번이라고 이름을 붙혀서 구분하자는 것인데, 써놨듯이 그냥 아무렇게나 붙이면 된다. 사실 정의처럼 써놓긴 했지만 잘 정의된 개념은 아닌데, 다음의 정리를 증명하기 위한 중간 과정에 불과하기 때문이다.

## Theorem 1
Let $L$ be the graph Laplacian of a graph $G$. Then we have:

**(i)** $L$ is positive semi-definite, i.e., each eigenvalue of $L$ is nonnegative.

**(ii)** $L$ has at least one zero eigenvalue; that is, $L$ is not invertible.

### Proof
**(i)** Let $B$ be the edge-incidence matrix of $G$. We claim that $L = B^TB$, that is, $L_{ij} = \sum_k B_{ki} B_{kj}$.

$\big[ (\because)$ If $i \neq j$, then the only non-zero terms in the sum will occur if both $B_{ki}$ and $B_{kj}$ are non-zero, i.e., if $e_k$ connects $v_i$ and $v_j$, in which case the product will have value $-1$. If $i = j$, then the sum is $\sum_{k} B_{ki}^2$, which has a term $+1$ for every edge connected to $v_i$, so the whole sum is just equal to $d_i$. It follows that $\sum_k B_{ki} B_{kj} = L_{ij}$, which means that $L = B^TB. \big]$

Now, let $\mathbb{v}_i$ be a normalized eigenvector of $L$ with eigenvalue $\lambda_i$. Then we have

$$\begin{align*}
\| B\mathbf{v}_i \|^2 &= \langle B\mathbf{v}_i, B\mathbf{v}_i \rangle \\
&= (B\mathbf{v}_i)^T (B\mathbf{v}_i) \\
&= \mathbf{v}_i^T B^T B \mathbf{v}_i \\
&= \mathbf{v}_i^T L \mathbf{v}_i \\
&= \lambda_i \| \mathbf{v}_i \|^2 \\
&= \lambda_i.
\end{align*}$$

so $\lambda_i \ge 0$. Hence, each eigenvalue of $L$ is nonnegative, which means that $L$ is positive semi-definite.

**(ii)** Let us denote $\mathbf{1} = [1 \,\, \cdots \,\, 1]^T$. Then we have that for each $i$,

$$\begin{align*}
[L \cdot \mathbf{1}]_i &= \sum_{j} L_{ij} \times 1 \\
&= \sum_j (\delta_{ij} d_i - A_{ij}) \\
&= d_i - d_i \\
&= 0.
\end{align*}$$

which implies that $L \cdot \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0} = 0 \cdot \mathbf{1}$. Thus, $\mathbf{0}$ is an eigenvalue of $L$ with eigenvector $\mathbf{1}$, and so $L$ is not invertible. $\blacksquare$

증명에서 (i)의 claim 부분을 보면 알겠지만, 에지의 양 끝을 어떤 방식으로 이름을 붙이던간에 어차피 우리가 관심있는 값은 $B_{ki}$와 $B_{kj}$의 곱, 혹은 제곱이기 때문에 항상 일정한 값이 나오게 된다. 따라서 $L = B^TB$라는 결론을 이끌어 내기 위해서 어떤 방식으로 edge-incidence matrix를 정의하던지 상관이 없게 된다.

## Theorem 2
Let $G$ be a graph which is divided up into $c$ different components of sizes $n_1, n_2, \cdots, n_c$, and let $L$ be the graph Laplacian of $G$.

**(i)** $L$ has exactly $c$ zero eigenvalues.

**(ii)** Let $0 = \lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \cdots \le \lambda_n$ be the eigenvalues of $L$ in increasing order. Then the second eigenvalue $\lambda_2$, called ***algebraic connectivity*** of $G$, is nonzero $\iff$ the graph $G$ is connected, i.e., it consists of a single component.

### Proof
**(i)** For convinience, let us number the vertices of the graph so that  the first $n_1$ vertices are those of the first component, the next $n_2$ are those of the second component, and so forth. With this choice the Laplacian of the network will be block diagonal, looking something like this:

$$L =
\begin{bmatrix}
    \boxed{\phantom{\Huge O}} & 0 & \cdots \\
    0 & \boxed{\phantom{\Huge O}} & \cdots \\
    \vdots & \vdots & \ddots
\end{bmatrix}.$$

Note that each block in the Laplacian is the Laplacian of the corresponding component. By Theorem 1 (ii), there are $c$ linearly independent vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{v}_c$ such that $L\mathbf{v}_i = \mathbf{0}$, where

$$\mathbf{v}_i = [0 \cdots 0 \,\, \underbrace{1 \cdots 1}_{n_i \text{ entries}} \,\, 0 \cdots 0]^T.$$

We claim that these $c$ vectors form a basis for the null space $\ker(L)$ of $L$, which is the eigenspace corresponding to the eigenvalue $0$.

$\big[ (\because)$ Let $N = n_1 + n_2 + \cdots + n_c$. Then $L$ is a $N \times N$ real matrix. For each $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^N$, we obtain:

$$\begin{align*}
\mathbf{x}^T L \mathbf{x} &= \sum_{i} x_i [L\mathbf{x}]_i \\
&= \sum_i x_i \sum_j L_{ij} x_j \\
&= \sum_i x_i \sum_j (\delta_{ij}d_i - A_{ij}) x_j \\
&= \sum_{i, j} \delta_{ij} d_i x_i x_j - \sum_{i, j} A_{ij} x_i x_j \\
&= \sum_i d_i x_i^2 - \sum_{i, j} A_{ij} x_i x_j \\
&= \sum_{i, j} A_{ij} x_i^2 - \sum_{i, j} A_{ij} x_i x_j \\
&= \frac{1}{2}\left[ \sum_{i, j} A_{ij} (x_i - x_j)^2 \right] \\
&= \sum_{\{i, j\} \in E(G)} (x_i - x_j)^2.
\end{align*}$$

Let $\mathbf{x} \in \ker(L)$. Then $L\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$, and so $\mathbf{x}^T L \mathbf{x} = 0$. By above result, it follows that $x_i = x_j$ for all $\{i, j\} \in E(G)$.

For any component $C_k$, let $u$ and $v$ be any two vertices in $V(C_k)$. Since they are connected by a path in $C_k$, it follows that $x_u = x_v$. This implies that the restriction of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ to the vertices of $C_k$ is constant. Thus, we can express the vector $\mathbf{x} \in \ker(L)$ as the linear combination of $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{v}_c \}$:

$$\mathbf{x} = X_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + X_c \mathbf{v}_c$$

for some constants $X_1, \cdots, X_c$. Hence, the set $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{v}_c \}$ forms a basis for $\ker(L)$.$\big]$

Since $L$ is Hermitian, it is diagonalizable, which means that the geometric multiplicity $c$ is equal to the algebraic multiplicity. Thus, $L$ has exactly $c$ zero eigenvalues.

**(ii)** By (i), the algebraic multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue is exactly $c$. If the graph $G$ is connected, then $c = 1$. This means only the first eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ is zero, forcing the second eigenvalue $\lambda_2 > 0$. Conversely, if $G$ is disconnected, then $c \ge 2$, which means there are at least two zero eigenvalues (i.e., $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = 0$). Thus, $\lambda_2 \neq 0$ if and only if $G$ is connected. $\blacksquare$
